Next month the 26th marks the first anniversary of the Tai Po Wang Fuk Court fire. The independent committee investigating the fire is expected to submit its report to the Chief Executive before the end of October. Recent reports indicated that the government has launched a departmental head accountability system to investigate the administrative responsibility for the fire and redeployed administrative officers to assist. Chief Executive John Lee today (the 6th) did not respond to whether the mechanism had been activated, stating that the government has made a series of deployments and will implement reforms and pursue accountability as soon as possible after the report is submitted. The luxury residence One Stanley in Stanley was exposed for reinforcement bars not matching the plans. Lee stated that the Buildings Department is investigating the case and has requested the Development Bureau to monitor the investigation. As multiple projects have been exposed for problems one after another, he said he attaches great importance to the construction quality of building works in Hong Kong, which relates to the professionalism, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and the government will strictly enforce the law.

Nearly a year after the Wang Fuk Court fire, the independent committee is expected to submit its report before the end of October. (File photo)

Earlier media reports stated that two administrative officers, former Deputy Secretary for Security Mok Kwan-yu and Commissioner for Sports Choi Kin-bun, would provide support to an investigation小组 under the Public Service Commission, specifically responsible for preliminary work on administrative accountability.

Before attending the Executive Council meeting today, Chief Executive John Lee met the press and was asked whether the reports were true, and whether activating the departmental head accountability system to investigate responsibility means that even with a report, results regarding official accountability would not be available immediately, and how long the public would have to wait.

Lee stated that he had made it clear from the start that after the independent committee submits its report, he would actively study and follow up on recommendations, implement reforms and announce details. He did not directly respond to whether administrative officers had been redeployed to prepare preliminary investigation work, only saying that "the government has made a series of deployments during this period," emphasising that after the report is submitted, based on its contents, "comprehensive reforms will be implemented as soon as possible in the short term, and accountability will be pursued," with detailed announcements to be made at that time.

Lee stated that after the independent committee submits its report, reforms will be implemented and accountability pursued as soon as possible based on the report's contents. (File photo)

Lee also reiterated multiple times that improvement measures are urgent, so when delivering the Policy Address in September, seven priority improvement measures were announced, including banning smoking at construction sites, strengthening regulation of fire service installations, strengthening disciplinary action against professionals and contractors, improving compliance in owners' corporations, studying the criminalisation of bid-rigging, providing tendering and evaluation services for the first time, establishing prequalification lists for consultants and contractors, and studying solutions to better assist the public on matters involving professional expertise in works projects.

According to records, the Public Service Commission is an independent statutory advisory body that advises the Chief Executive on civil service appointments, promotions and disciplinary matters. The departmental head accountability system was proposed by Chief Executive Lee in last year's Policy Address, establishing a two-tier investigation mechanism based on the severity of departmental issues. If the issue is less serious or involves a single incident, the first-tier investigation will be conducted by the departmental head. If a department has serious problems, or involves extensive or repeated systemic issues, or may involve the role of the departmental head, a second-tier investigation will be conducted by an investigation group led by the Public Service Commission.

The luxury residence One Stanley was exposed for having units with reinforcement bars not matching the plans. Lee stated he would not comment on cases still under investigation, and has requested the Development Bureau to monitor the Buildings Department's investigation.

One Stanley "reinforcement bar irregularities" – Development Bureau requested to monitor investigation

Recently, building works have been exposed for problems one after another, including lift shaft tilting at the new block of Queen Mary Hospital, concrete samples at a Tung Chung public housing estate not meeting strength standards, and floor slab reinforcement bars at the Stanley luxury residence One Stanley not matching the plans. Lee was asked whether there are problems with construction and even project supervision.

He responded on the One Stanley project issue, stating that the Buildings Department is seriously investigating the case, "ascertaining whether construction quality and supervision were adequate, and will handle it strictly in accordance with the law." As the investigation is ongoing, he would not comment on case details, and has requested the Development Bureau to monitor the investigation. However, he emphasised that he attaches importance to construction quality in Hong Kong's building works, "paying attention to whether professionals related to the works have duly supervised, and whether contractors have violated regulations during construction," and stated that this concerns the professionalism, quality and safety of Hong Kong's construction industry, and the government will definitely enforce the law strictly.

He has also requested the Development Bureau to enhance legal regulatory requirements and penalties for overall building works, to ensure the deterrent effect of legislation, severely punish relevant personnel who violate regulations, and safeguard the professionalism, quality and safety of Hong Kong's building works. The Development Bureau will submit proposed amendments to the Buildings Ordinance this year to strengthen regulation and enhance the disciplinary system and penalties, and the authorities will推进 the related work at full speed.

Recent attention has been drawn to the difficulty faced by nursing graduates in finding jobs. Lee stated that demand for nurses has long existed, and pointed out that the Hospital Authority currently has over 3,000 nursing vacancies that graduates may apply for. (File photo)

Executive Council member Tommy Cheung criticises "unions putting on an act" – Lee states demand has long existed

Discussion about the difficulty of finding nursing jobs has heated up recently. The source was a radio phone-in programme after the Policy Address, where a Mr Kwok, who claimed to be a psychiatric nurse in a disciplined service, said his application for deferred retirement was not approved, and that his daughter, a nursing graduate, was unemployed upon graduation, questioning the Hospital Authority's recruitment of Mainland medical personnel. Executive Council member Tommy Cheung subsequently questioned whether the unions were "putting on an act calling in," and stated he would raise his hand in support of importing talent from outside.

Reporters asked about the difficulty nursing graduates face in finding jobs, how to address the concentration of vacancies among experienced nurses, and how to respond to remarks by Executive Council members being accused of aggravating social divisions. Lee stated that in every industry, there are cases where graduates do not immediately seek employment for various reasons, or where recruiting organisations select the most suitable candidates, "resulting in situations where certain individuals are not hired." He emphasised that societal demand for nurses has always existed, particularly as Hong Kong's healthcare continues to develop and the population ages, "so recruitment numbers will ultimately inevitably reflect this existing demand." He also said, without naming names, that "there are different discussions in society on this aspect, which can help everyone clarify the issues through discussion."

Lee also stated that according to 2025/26 figures, there are approximately 4,000 potential nursing graduates, with about 2,500 actually applying to the Hospital Authority, meaning 1,500 applied for positions outside the Hospital Authority. The Hospital Authority currently still has over 3,000 nursing vacancies, "nursing graduates can apply, and there is an opportunity to be hired."

Secretary for Health Professor Lo Chung-mau earlier accepted interviews with multiple media outlets to clarify that the government's recruitment policy definitely prioritises local talent. Lee also reiterated that based on the current number of nurses in the Hospital Authority, "99.8% are locally trained nurses in Hong Kong," clearly implementing the policy of prioritising local talent for employment. He also pointed out that currently 40% of nurses work in the public healthcare system, with the remaining 60% in other healthcare positions, such as community nursing, elderly care, rehabilitation services, and private medical institutions. He emphasised that societal demand for nurses has long existed. The government will, based on healthcare service needs, exchange views with the industry and academia, and do a good job in planning for healthcare training and manpower development.
